- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.27) over recent days, model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid underestimating rebound.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model often overshoots and fails to correct; reduce forecast peak by 5–10% and add a slight downward slope afterward.
- If sentiment is high (≥0.80) and price is trending up, model frequently overestimates future gains; cap forecast at 1–2% above recent high or use moving average smoothing.
- Model underestimates mean reversion in volatile periods; if sentiment is mixed or neutral (0.53), add a 2–3% upward bias to forecast to account for reversion to prior mean.
- For 30-day horizon, model often lags by 1–3 days in capturing sentiment-driven shifts; shift forecast 1–2 days ahead if sentiment turns sharply positive or negative.
- When sentiment is negative and price is falling, model tends to underestimate the drop; add 2–5% downward bias to forecast to reflect stronger sell-off.
- If sentiment is consistently positive but price is flat or declining, model overestimates upside; reduce forecast by 3–5% to avoid overconfidence bias.
